name: Calcium

lead: Calcium is the most abundant mineral in the human body, with the great majority stored in bones and teeth, where it provides rigidity. It is obtained from dairy, fortified foods, leafy greens and supplements.

Adequate intake supports bone mineralisation and peak bone mass, which matters for the skeleton overall. Supplementation helps mainly when dietary intake is low; extra calcium does not reshape facial bone in people who already get enough.

paras: Calcium is deposited as hydroxyapatite in the bone matrix, while a small circulating fraction signals muscle contraction, nerve transmission and clotting. Blood levels are tightly regulated by parathyroid hormone, vitamin D and calcitonin, with bone acting as a reservoir that is drawn on when intake falls short.

Excess intake from supplements can cause constipation, kidney stones and hypercalcaemia, and some studies have raised questions about cardiovascular effects of high-dose supplements. Dietary sources are preferred where possible, and calcium can interact with certain antibiotics and thyroid medicines.
